title: Regulating bridging loans through FCA rules
h1: Regulating bridging loans through FCA rules
summary: Blog article on how UK bridging loans fall under Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) regulation. As far as the search results reveal, the thesis is the regulated/unregulated split: a bridging loan is regulated when the property is inhabited, or will be inhabited, by the borrower or a family member, with the stated aim of making lenders and brokers act transparently and fairly. Concrete guidance surfaced: regulated bridging loans are restricted to a maximum term of 12 months and can only be used for a handful of reasons, renovation or refurbishment being one of the most common; regulated lenders are required to conduct an in-depth analysis of the property and the borrower; by contrast unregulated loans have no restraints on term length and can run from 1 month to 36 months; and on mixed-use property, if the borrower or a family member intends to live in the residential part, the loan becomes FCA-regulated, which severely restricts the number of lenders available. Caveat: the direct-URL search returned no content from this page, and the site: search summary pooled 'several Silver Oak Capital pages on this topic' (including /difference-between-regulated-unregulated-bridging-loans/ and /mixed-use-property-finance/), so point-level attribution to this specific article is not confirmed. No case-study deal data applies (this is an article, not a case study).
